name: Hollow cheeks via chewing then fat loss

image.caption: Hollow cheeks via chewing then fat loss

lead: This approach pairs masseter-focused chewing with body and facial fat loss to bring out the cheekbones and the hollow below them. The goal is hollow cheeks with a more visible cheekbone and jaw.

Proponents describe the hollow as coming from cheekbone projection, jaw angle and masseter size, which become visible when facial fat is low. Wikipedia notes the buccal fat pad also contributes to cheek fullness. No clinical study of the combination was found, and forum members disagree about the look itself.

paras: People chew firm gum or tough foods to work the masseter while reducing body fat through diet and training over weeks to months, and track the cheeks and jaw in photos taken in consistent lighting.
No harms were documented for the combination in the sources reviewed. Medical literature associates very hollow cheeks with aging or lipodystrophy, conditions treated with volume restoration.

angle.text: Forum posters build the masseter with chewing and lower body and facial fat so cheekbones and jaw structure show more, creating hollow cheeks. They describe the hollow as coming from bone and muscle, revealed by less soft tissue. No studies test the combination.

lead: "Hollow cheeks via chewing then fat loss" is a looksmaxxing approach that combines masseter-focused chewing with a reduction in body and facial fat, with the aim of showing cheekbone and jaw structure. Proponents describe hollow cheeks as the shadowed area below the cheekbones, produced by bone, muscle and the amount of soft tissue over them. The look it aims at is a leaner, more sculpted midface with a defined jaw angle and a visible shadow under the cheekbones.

The sequence matters to people who use it: chewing is meant to build the masseter, the jaw-closing muscle at the angle of the jaw, and fat loss is meant to reveal that muscle and the cheekbones above it. Wikipedia notes that habitual clenching, grinding and constant gum chewing are associated with an enlarged masseter, which can change the lower face [1]. Fat loss is the other half: lowering overall body fat is the route most forum members describe for reducing cheek fullness.

The approach sits beside several other practices aimed at the same look, including buccal fat removal surgery, jaw exercisers and hard gum, and weight-loss medications. Published research touches each part separately. A 2024 randomised trial of gum-chewing training measured the masseter [2]; MRI studies have charted how facial fat changes with weight loss in patients with HIV-related conditions [3]; and plastic surgery literature covers cheek hollowing from ageing and its correction [4][5][6][7]. No published trial has tested chewing followed by fat loss as a combined method for cheek hollowing.

paras: Looksmax.org members describe two broad sources of hollow cheeks: those formed by zygomatic bone projection and those formed by the masseter muscle and jaw angle, with lighting changing how pronounced they appear. In threads on the topic, members also point to a low level of facial fat as a precondition, and some ask whether hollow cheeks can be achieved without dieting.
Others dispute the goal. One thread argues hollow cheeks can look overly gaunt and that cheek dimples with a thin fat layer look better.

Two things determine how a cheek hollow appears in the forum framework: the structure beneath (cheekbone projection and jaw angle) and the soft tissue over it. Because facial fat does not shrink independently of body fat for most people, members who want the look typically describe losing weight overall; members who do not want to lose weight ask about alternatives, including buccal fat removal.

The masseter is a thick, roughly quadrilateral muscle with superficial, deep and coronoid heads, innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, and its job is to close and slightly protrude the jaw. Wikipedia reports that masseter hypertrophy is associated with habitual clenching and grinding (bruxism) and with constant gum chewing, usually bilateral, painless and soft, and that it can alter the look of the lower face and cause asymmetry when it is one-sided. It adds that people often seek care because of comments about their appearance, and that the condition can coexist with temporomandibular joint problems [1].

That is the physiological basis proponents rely on when they describe chewing as a way to thicken the jaw angle. The same article carries a notice that its claims need more citations, and it does not state how much chewing is needed to change the muscle [1]. Forum threads describe various chewing routines but no trial measures their effect on cheek appearance.

A 2024 randomised controlled trial in the Journal of Oral Rehabilitation assigned 58 healthy adults to chew gum three times a day for six months or to a no-training control. Maximum bite force rose in the chewing group by three months, linked to a larger occlusal contact area, while masseter thickness and mandibular shape did not change meaningfully, according to the authors [2]. Forum members who chew hard gum or use resistance jaw trainers describe visible jaw-angle growth over months, though these reports are self-observations.

No studies found for chewing followed by fat loss as a combined method. Related studies are separate: a 2024 randomised trial of gum-chewing training [2], an MRI study of facial fat change with weight loss and lipoatrophy [3], and plastic surgery literature on restoring cheek volume. Related medical literature is about restoring lost cheek volume: reports on microliposuction and fat transplantation in the aging face [4], collagen fillers used to augment hollow cheeks [5], reconstruction in partial lipodystrophy where extremely hollow cheeks are a feature [6], and a corrective surgery for hollow cheeks [7]. These address volume replacement, not chewing or deliberate fat loss. A 1990 report described microliposuction of facial fat and fat transplantation in aging faces, noting that fat loss with age can produce hollow cheeks and deep grooves [4]. A prosthodontic case report described a cheek plumper prosthesis for hollow cheeks in a dental patient [8].

The fat-loss half of the method rests on the idea that facial fat shrinks along with body fat. MRI work in people with HIV-related lipoatrophy, wasting and weight change found that superficial facial fat fell in the weight-loss group and in lipoatrophy, mainly in the cheeks, and rose substantially in those who gained weight [3]. That study measured clinical populations, not people dieting for appearance, so it describes the direction of change rather than how much a given person will lean out.

Cheek fullness varies by person. Members describe some people as keeping full cheeks at low body fat and others hollowing early, and they attribute this to the buccal fat pad and bone structure. Wikipedia reports that the buccal fat pad is implicated in hollow cheeks and that its intermediate lobe loses volume between childhood and adulthood [9].

Recent reviews also discuss the facial effects of rapid weight loss on GLP-1 receptor agonist medications, sometimes called "Ozempic face" in media, describing reduced facial fat and sagging skin [10].

sections.h: Buccal fat removal and other alternatives
paras: Members who do not want to lose body weight ask about buccal fat removal, a cosmetic operation that takes out part of the buccal fat pad through the inside of the mouth. Wikipedia describes it as usually done under local anaesthetic, taking about 30 minutes, with swelling lasting days and final results taking up to three months [11]. It reports that the American Society of Plastic Surgeons recorded 4,543 procedures in 2022 and that a 2022 New York Times report linked rising interest to Twitter and TikTok; Chrissy Teigen publicly disclosed having the procedure in 2021 [11].

The same article lists risks including injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and to the parotid duct, notes the removal is permanent, and says the cheeks may look gaunt as natural volume loss occurs with age [11]. Fillers, fat grafting and dermal fat grafts are described as options for restoring volume [11][4][5].

Wikipedia lists hollow cheeks among the facial features looksmaxxers check for, alongside a defined jawline [12]. It places weight management within softmaxxing and extreme low body fat dieting within hardmaxxing, and notes that some people obtain GLP-1 drugs through unregulated channels [12]. Forum threads on the topic ask how the look arises, whether it requires dieting, and whether it is desirable at all.

Wikipedia describes the buccal fat pad as a deep cheek fat mass that contributes to hollow cheeks and the nasolabial fold, but not to jowls [9]. It lists proposed roles in suckling and as a gliding pad for chewing muscles [9]. It does not discuss whether chewing changes cheek shape.

The same article notes that the buccal fat pad's intermediate lobe seems to lose significant volume between childhood and adulthood, and that removal of the pad is sometimes used to reduce cheek prominence, a procedure with a recognised risk to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid ducts [9]. It describes the pad as distinct from the malar fat pad just under the skin of the cheek and from jowl fat [9].

lore.intro: Hollow cheeks are a frequent topic on looksmax.org, with members describing multiple routes to them and disagreeing about how desirable they are.

claims.claim: Hollow cheeks come from bone and masseter structure, with fat loss revealing them.
Overly hollow cheeks can look gaunt, and a thin fat layer may be preferable.
Chewing hard gum or resistance trainers thickens the jaw angle and improves the lower face.
Losing body fat is what makes cheeks hollow.
Buccal fat removal is a shortcut to the same look without dieting.
Rapid weight loss on GLP-1 drugs gives a sculpted face.

timeline.event: Lorenz Heister first describes the buccal fat pad, as glandular tissue [11].
Xavier Bichat identifies the structure as fat, giving the pad its alternative name [11].
Plastic surgery journals publish reports on corrective surgery for hollow cheeks and on facial reconstruction in partial lipodystrophy [6][7].
A report describes microliposuction and fat transplantation for the ageing face, including hollow cheeks [4].
MRI study charts facial fat change in HIV-related lipoatrophy, weight loss and weight gain [3].
Chrissy Teigen discloses having buccal fat removal [11].
The New York Times reports growing social-media-driven interest in buccal fat removal; 4,543 procedures recorded by US plastic surgeons [11].
Randomised trial of six months of gum-chewing training reports higher bite force with no meaningful change in masseter thickness [2].
